speakers: Alvaro And Jen From The Ure

claims.claim_text: Semiconductor vendors sell fixed-function parts that are ordinary microcontrollers with firmware preloaded; Microchip's MCP2200 USB-to-serial device is a PIC18F14K50 programmed at the factory, which lets the vendor create a proven, documented product from existing stock without a new silicon design.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's an 18F 14K50 USB chip with just some firmware programmed in
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Agilent, Analog, Cold Fusion - Funding Fusion Is Not Futile

claims.claim_text: On platforms where the operating system is developed separately from the hardware, an upstream release cannot reach a device until the handset maker integrates it with the low-level firmware specific to that model and republishes it, so update latency and fragmentation are a structural consequence of the split rather than a defect of any one vendor.
claims.quote_verbatim: you then have to wait for your manufacturer to actually take the release, package it up, talk down to the low-level firmware, whatever's specific to their phone
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Instrument capabilities held back for market-segmentation reasons can later be released as a firmware update to hardware already in the field; Agilent added arbitrary waveform generation to its 3000 series oscilloscopes this way roughly nine months after saying the feature had been withheld to protect its function generator line.
claims.quote_verbatim: They have released new firmware today for the 3000 series and it's got a whole bunch of new things
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Silego, ADCs & Seismic Detection - Dave's Dingo Dystocia

claims.claim_text: Where an instrument's bandwidth grade is set in firmware rather than in hardware, the difference between models is a licensing decision, and a price cut that equalises the two grades makes the firmware modification pointless because the higher-bandwidth unit costs the same.
claims.quote_verbatim: they didn't want to do the firmware hack themselves they're like yeah i'm just going to sell my scope and buy buy the other one
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: A platform vendor that wants third parties to build add-on boards can still reserve for itself the accessories that require changes to the platform firmware, such as camera interfaces, because those cannot be supported without coordinated firmware releases.
claims.quote_verbatim: I think we're going to restrict ourselves to the kind of technical ones, which is basically camera and camera and just like the things that require the firmware
claims.speaker: Eben Upton
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Eben Upton - Morbus Moilsome MakerFaire

claims.claim_text: Bringing up a new chip on a development platform and exercising it with real commands produces working driver code that can be handed straight to the firmware effort, so the evaluation step doubles as the first increment of the product's firmware.
claims.quote_verbatim: once I, you know, if I actually exercise the chip by throwing commands at it, then I'm already halfway there when I'm on the firmware side, I can just hand over this code that does work
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Armstrong, Camenzind & Museums - Outstanding Oneirophoros Obituaries

claims.claim_text: Committing early to a real board rather than a breadboard mock-up means the eventual production layout is largely finished and the firmware has been developed on the final platform, so neither has to be redone; the counter-argument, that hardware must be proven before committing to a PCB, is usually a budget constraint rather than a technical one.
claims.quote_verbatim: your code's done because you haven't hacked code from here or there, you know, it's all on the final platform you're going to be using
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Armstrong, Camenzind & Museums - Outstanding Oneirophoros Obituaries

claims.claim_text: Test instruments split their processing between firmware, which is fast enough for real-time work but inflexible, and a host or embedded PC running the user interface, where sophisticated post-processing is practical; higher-end instruments often carry both a PC for the interface and a separate processor for number crunching.
claims.quote_verbatim: more and more gets pushed into firmware and things like that to do more kind of real-time fast hardware-based processing. But you're limited in flexibility of what you can do there
claims.speaker: Alan Wolke

claims.claim_text: Production programming is best done from a single manufacturing image that contains the bootloader, the application firmware and any per-unit data such as a unique identifier, so the factory performs one programming operation per board rather than a sequence of separate loads.
claims.quote_verbatim: You program this one manufacturing image into the device, and it's got bootloader firmware, unique ID, whatever you've got to put in there. It's all in there in one programming step
claims.speaker: Ian Lesnet
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ian Lesnet - Bus Buccaneer Builder

claims.claim_text: Bootloaders that rely on a microcontroller's internal oscillator can fail on particular silicon revisions where that oscillator is not stable enough to hold the serial bit rate, a defect that only appears once boards are being programmed in volume.
claims.quote_verbatim: there was a little quirk in one revision of that silicon where the internal oscillator wasn't stable enough
claims.speaker: Ian Lesnet
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ian Lesnet - Bus Buccaneer Builder

claims.claim_text: Vendor-supplied peripheral stacks can carry licence terms that permit use but forbid redistributing the source, which forces an open project to keep the vendor code in a separate tree and ship an incomplete source release that will not compile in one step.
claims.quote_verbatim: it comes with a license clause that says you can use it freely, but you can't actually include the source when you distribute it
claims.speaker: Ian Lesnet
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ian Lesnet - Bus Buccaneer Builder

claims.claim_text: Moving from an external USB-to-serial bridge to a microcontroller with an integrated USB peripheral removes the protocol overhead that made bulk operations slow, but transfers responsibility for the USB device stack into the firmware.
claims.quote_verbatim: we used a bigger PIC chip with more pins, four times more storage space, and most importantly, an integrated USB peripheral
claims.speaker: Ian Lesnet
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ian Lesnet - Bus Buccaneer Builder

claims.claim_text: Component obsolescence is far more disruptive than in the discrete-logic era: replacing a 74-series part meant accepting a logic change, whereas replacing a modern integrated part invalidates firmware and the software layered on top of it, so the engineering change propagates through the whole system.
claims.quote_verbatim: now there's so much software built on top of it, right? There's firmware and then there's software built on top of that. And it just propagates through the system
claims.episode_title: eReaders, datasheets & board assembly - Yearly Yeasty Yapping

claims.claim_text: In a small vehicle team one engineer may write the firmware for both the drivetrain and the braking system and also drive the car, so a change in one subsystem can be traded against its effect on the other directly; large organisations split those subsystems across teams and mediate the same trade through specification and meetings.
claims.quote_verbatim: the same guy who worked on the firmware for the drivetrain is also working on the firmware for the analog braking system
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Intel, EPA & Brown Field - Google's Ground Gurgitation

claims.claim_text: Continuous integration for firmware requires attached target hardware, a programming path and an automated agent that compiles each commit, installs it and runs a test procedure, which makes it substantially harder to set up than for a pure software project; its value is that a change that breaks something is caught immediately rather than a month later.
claims.quote_verbatim: you have to have some kind of a setup where you have the attached hardware and you have programming system and some kind of automated tool to take whatever's been committed to the repo and, like, automatically compile it and install it and run some kind of test procedure
claims.speaker: Michael Ossmann
claims.episode_title: Interview with Michael Ossmann - Gifted Grimgribber Grokker

claims.claim_text: Adding a second processor to a design adds a second firmware image to maintain, and updating it in the field usually requires the main processor to relay code to it; a power loss during that relay can leave the secondary device unprogrammed, which is why a slower single-processor design talking over SPI is often preferred.
claims.quote_verbatim: then what happens if it's out in the field and you, and you find a bug, you're screwed, right? I mean, I mean, usually one of the processors has to pass the code to the other processor. Please don't lose power during that time
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Elecia White - Wirewove Worshipping Wookieist?

claims.claim_text: When a board is revised, keeping the connector and pin assignments compatible is only half the job; if the firmware also diverges between revisions the maintenance burden multiplies, because every subsequent change must be made and tested in each variant.
claims.quote_verbatim: as long as you don't start diverging the firmware as well, then you're usually in good shape, right? You don't have to maintain multiple versions
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: B Plus Boards and D Minus Cities - Uneath Urban Ubication

claims.claim_text: A field-updatable device typically holds a small bootloader in flash that runs first at every boot, checks the application image for validity and only then transfers execution to it; the application in turn provides a way to re-enter the bootloader so a new image can be accepted.
claims.quote_verbatim: You'll have a little bootloader, which is a small program that resides in Flash. And when the device boots up, it runs this bootloader first. And normally what the bootloader does is it checks the application for validity
claims.speaker: Trey German
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Trey German - Launchpad Laden Lodesman

claims.claim_text: The transport used to deliver a firmware update is incidental to the bootloader design: CAN, USB or a plain UART all work, and the choice follows whatever communication path already exists in the product. In vehicles, CAN is used because the modules cannot be removed and reprogrammed through their JTAG headers.
claims.quote_verbatim: the new application software is loaded over some type of communication network. In this case, it was CAN. But this can be done with USB, just a simple UART. Really, any way that you can get information into a chip
claims.speaker: Trey German
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Trey German - Launchpad Laden Lodesman

claims.claim_text: Product team composition has shifted away from hardware: where a design once needed several hardware engineers, teams now run closer to one hardware engineer to four firmware engineers to five software engineers, because functionality that can be changed after shipping is worth more than functionality fixed in the board.
claims.quote_verbatim: one hardware engineer, four firmware people, and, you know, five software
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Get Smart About Automation - Caducous Cyborg Concerns

claims.claim_text: Published time breakdowns from one open-hardware manufacturer put firmware at only about five percent of engineering effort, against 2.5 percent each for board design and breadboarding and ten percent for revising and reworking prototypes; writing libraries consumed roughly three times as much time as firmware, because the library work is what makes subsequent firmware quick.
claims.quote_verbatim: revising and reworking prototypes is 10%. Board design is 2.5%. Breadboarding is 2.5%. Firmware is only 5
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Get Smart About Automation - Caducous Cyborg Concerns

claims.claim_text: Firmware can be written and self-tested against a schedule before the board returns from manufacture, so that bring-up starts from complete code rather than from nothing; this is the standard answer to the software team idling while hardware is fabricated.
claims.quote_verbatim: I had the firmware actually ready to go, complete, sort of like tested and tested within itself, even though I had no hardware to work on before I got my board back
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Prepping For Hoverboards - Gallionic GitHub Gabble

claims.claim_text: A defective field-update path can brick the device it is meant to service: one 3D printer had a known bug in which attempting a firmware update erased the part, and recovery required disassembling the machine and reprogramming the microcontroller directly through its in-circuit header.
claims.quote_verbatim: I bricked the firmware in my MakerBot, right? It's got a famous bug where, you know, if you try to update the firmware, it just nukes it
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Prepping For Hoverboards - Gallionic GitHub Gabble

claims.claim_text: The Raspberry Pi HAT specification requires an EEPROM on the add-on board describing the mechanical form and how the pins are used, so that platform firmware reads it at boot and configures the interface automatically rather than requiring the user to declare the hardware.
claims.quote_verbatim: You put an E-squared PROM on your hat board, and then the firmware on the Raspberry Pi is able to configure itself based on that E-squared PROM information
claims.speaker: Matt Richardson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Matt Richardson - Raspberry Risorgimento Regent

claims.claim_text: Extracting a device's secret does not require reading its firmware: a side-channel attack on a chip that holds a key, including the bitstream-decryption keys used by FPGA vendors, can recover the key from a part that contains no application code at all.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you just give me a chip, it doesn't have the firmware in it or anything, then I can do a side-channel attack on that chip to figure out what the secret key that's programmed into it
claims.speaker: Colin O'Flynn
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Colin O'Flynn - Aspirated Adamantine Attacks

claims.claim_text: Ordering microcontrollers pre-programmed from the distributor is the standard answer for boards with no in-circuit programming header, which is common on small packages where every pin is committed; the designer sends the firmware file and the parts arrive ready to place.
claims.quote_verbatim: if people haven't put an in-circuit serial programming header on their board
claims.speaker: Chris Church
claims.episode_title: An interview with Macrofab - Macro Manufacturing Mechanization

claims.claim_text: Some low-power devices that harvest their link from ambient radio require a modified access point whose firmware transmits continuously at the full one watt rather than in the usual duty-cycled bursts, so the system depends on non-standard infrastructure firmware rather than on any commodity router.
claims.quote_verbatim: They have to get a special wifi router that had special firmware that was modified to always continuously transmit it the full one watt power
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Consolidate All The Things - Zonked Zelotic Zaitech

claims.claim_text: Emissions and safety compliance can be defeated in firmware rather than in hardware: Volkswagen shipped code that detected when the vehicle was on a test cycle and changed behaviour accordingly, an approach that is invisible to inspection of the hardware and was applied across roughly half a million vehicles.
claims.quote_verbatim: let's just hack our firmware, put in a secret bit of firmware that detects when
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Modern evaluation-kit software generates the register initialisation sequence for a part, so a customer can blue-wire the new device into a previous-generation product, tune it through the kit's interface, dump the resulting settings and hand that configuration to the firmware engineer to implement.
claims.quote_verbatim: the GUIs that come with the eval kits now, they help. Oh, yeah. You know, they'll give you the initialization script
claims.speaker: Dafydd Roche

claims.claim_text: Shipping a product whose firmware only just fits the available memory is a serious mistake, because any later bug fix or feature must then displace existing code; selecting the part with headroom, such as a 128 kB device rather than a 64 kB one, is cheaper than the assembly-language optimisation the alternative eventually forces.
claims.quote_verbatim: that's probably the worst thing you can do is actually go into production with a product where your firmware just fits
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Smart-card piracy worked by physically opening the card and dumping its firmware so the behaviour could be emulated on a different card, producing functional clones without ever obtaining the original source code.
claims.quote_verbatim: basically dumping the firmware off of it so that they can then emulate it on a different smart card
claims.speaker: Dmitry Nedospasov

claims.claim_text: A general-purpose USB peripheral is really three coupled deliverables: the device firmware, the host-side library, and the protocol over USB that joins them; designing the protocol to keep the device general rather than special-casing each use is the hard part.
claims.quote_verbatim: getting that Python interface working well and getting a protocol over the USB that we like and getting firmware, uh, all working together to make this as general purpose as possible, uh, has been a challenge
claims.speaker: Michael Ossmann
claims.episode_title: Impedance Matching with Michael Ossmann and Dmitry Nedospazov

claims.claim_text: Extending MicroPython means adding a C source file to the open-source tree and marking its functions with macros that declare how they are exposed to the interpreter, then compiling the whole tree to a binary image that is flashed to the board; the REPL that results is itself part of that firmware rather than a layer above it.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's certain macros that you have to include in there to tell Python, okay, you know, this C function should be exposed in this way to Python
claims.speaker: Tony DiCola

claims.claim_text: When a microcontroller has fewer hardware PWM channels than the design needs, the shortfall is made up in software, which consumes processor time and is a common reason a part ends up tapped out; here eight PWM channels were required for bottom-mounted RGB indicators against fewer hardware channels available.
claims.quote_verbatim: which is more PWM channels than the AT tiny has. So it's done in software
claims.speaker: Zach Fredin

claims.claim_text: Hardware without firmware has no function, which makes the firmware author a first-class contributor rather than a downstream implementer; on complex projects that role spans the whole stack from bare-metal bootloaders up to network services.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you build hardware without firmware, it's just a shiny object that has no use
claims.speaker: Bunnie Huang

claims.claim_text: Where a vendor sells extra instrument bandwidth as a licence key, the underlying hardware is already capable and the restriction is a bit set in firmware, so the same physical unit can be unlocked by modifying that state.
claims.quote_verbatim: they sell a license key option for 100 megahertz bandwidth
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Look at nature and meet nerds

claims.claim_text: Agricultural equipment can enforce authorised repair through firmware at the individual component level: a replacement part that the owner has already bought and installed will not operate until a dealer representative approves it, so the constraint is a software interlock rather than a mechanical or electrical one.
claims.quote_verbatim: they have, like, firmware control at each component level

claims.claim_text: Opening an arbitrary consumer device typically reveals several immediately accessible attack surfaces, such as an exposed firmware image or a live JTAG or debugger interface, and the tools to exploit them are inexpensive; the security of off-the-shelf products has nevertheless improved measurably over a five-year window of hands-on training work.
claims.quote_verbatim: in the past five years of doing trainings and working with a lot of consumer off-the-shelf products, I've seen an actual improvement in the security of these things
claims.speaker: Joe Fitzpatrick

claims.claim_text: Attacks on embedded devices are chosen by cost rather than sophistication: network fuzzing, opening the case for debug headers, extracting firmware from flash, and silicon-level side-channel or decapping attacks each carry very different cost, time and skill requirements, and the cheapest route wins. The cheapest route of all is frequently downloading the firmware image from the vendor's own website.
claims.quote_verbatim: I talk about in class, like, oh, here's eight ways to go dump firmware. But then what's the easiest way to get the firmware? You just go to the vendor's website and download it
claims.speaker: Joe Fitzpatrick

claims.claim_text: USB-C did not reduce the attack surface: any cable or adapter doing more than basic USB contains a microcontroller, and such devices are frequently shipped with direct firmware update left enabled, so an adapter can have its firmware dumped and replaced by whoever holds it.
claims.quote_verbatim: Every device you plug into USB-C now needs to be smart. Any cable that you plug in that does anything beyond basic USB has essentially a microcontroller in it
claims.speaker: Joe Fitzpatrick

claims.claim_text: The usual objective of hardware attack work is to convert a hardware problem into a software one: get the firmware off the device, understand it, and from then on operate entirely in software to make the device do something it was not intended to do.
claims.quote_verbatim: I want to get firmware off and then use the firmware to figure out how I can make it a software problem
claims.speaker: Joe Fitzpatrick

claims.claim_text: Two products with different radio front ends were kept in a single firmware repository, so one clone of the tree builds the image for either board; the integration was done after the fact once the second product's firmware had been rushed to completion for an event.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can download, uh, you know, the, the, or, you know, clone our Git repo and compile firmware for either the HackRF one or the radio badge
claims.speaker: Michael Ossmann

claims.claim_text: Moving frequency tuning from the host into device firmware removes one USB round trip per tuning command, which is what makes a fast sweep across a six gigahertz range practical where a host-driven loop is limited by USB latency; a display fed by the host was limited to under twenty megahertz of instantaneous bandwidth.
claims.quote_verbatim: by doing the tuning in firmware instead of doing it on the host computer
claims.speaker: Michael Ossmann

claims.claim_text: A hardware engineer should be able to write the firmware for their own board, treating C or C++ as a basic tool of the trade, with a scripting language such as Python as the glue for quick instrumentation and data handling.
claims.quote_verbatim: you need to control your own firmware if you're a hardware engineer
claims.speaker: Akiba

claims.claim_text: Semihosting lets target firmware call file operations that are executed on the host running the debugger, so the embedded code can open and read a file that exists only on the development machine; combined with GDB's scripting, this is what makes the debugger a practical engine for factory test jigs.
claims.quote_verbatim: in your firmware and your target firmware, you just run open file name and this file is on the PC or on the computer where GDB is running
claims.speaker: Piotr Esden-Tempski

claims.claim_text: A contract manufacturer building a branded instrument may insist on retaining firmware maintenance itself rather than handing it to the brand owner, because the code becomes reusable across its other products; the brand owner's contribution is domain expertise in specification, test and debug.
claims.quote_verbatim: we want to develop code that we can use in other products
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Choosing the processor before the firmware exists fixes the memory budget by guesswork, so the firmware team inherits a hard constraint they had no input on and must reconcile it with a delivery date, usually by cutting features late.
claims.quote_verbatim: the decoupled hardware versus firmware decision
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: An interview with Alvaro and Jen from the URE Podcast

claims.claim_text: High-volume consumer products are often built from parts programmed before assembly, because the package is too small to carry a programming header, so the firmware must be finished earlier than for low-volume equipment where a connector allows programming just before shipment.
claims.quote_verbatim: you have to have your firmware ready ahead of time because it might be too small to have a programming header on there or at least put a bootloader on it
claims.episode_title: An interview with Alvaro and Jen from the URE Podcast

claims.claim_text: For connected consumer products the firmware flashed at the factory is a gold master burned three to four months before the unit reaches a customer, so the only requirements on it are that it boots, reaches the backend and successfully takes an update; the feature set can then land on day zero rather than at manufacture.
claims.quote_verbatim: my gold master, which gets flashed into a product three to four months ahead of when we actually have the product land in someone's hands, can boot up, connect to the backend server somehow, and get updated
claims.episode_title: An interview with Alvaro and Jen from the URE Podcast

claims.claim_text: Demand for firmware engineers in Silicon Valley has persistently exceeded supply, with recruiters unable to fill roles and hiring managers reporting difficulty finding merely competent candidates rather than exceptional ones; the practical bar for changing jobs is correspondingly low.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's hard to find a competent, I don't mean like incredible. I mean competent, solid firmware engineer
claims.episode_title: An interview with Alvaro and Jen from the URE Podcast

claims.claim_text: A device's protocol can be recovered without extracting its firmware by probing the bus between the microcontroller and the radio, recording the traffic and then driving the radio chip directly from a substitute microcontroller.
claims.quote_verbatim: instead of trying to dump the firmware in this case, I tapped the communications between the microcontroller and the radio chip
claims.speaker: Alvaro Prieto
claims.episode_title: An interview with Alvaro and Jen from the URE Podcast

claims.claim_text: A safe over-the-air update needs a second image slot: the new firmware is downloaded into the spare region, checksummed and verified there while the running image remains intact, and only then is control handed over, after which the old slot becomes the spare for the next update. Overwriting in place generally works exactly once.
claims.quote_verbatim: here's firmware A, I just downloaded firmware B, I did a check sum on firmware B, I stored it into memory
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Enabling a new update transport in a shipped product usually requires modifying the bootloader itself, which is the one component that cannot be safely changed by the update mechanism it implements.
claims.quote_verbatim: we could do it, but you'd have to change the bootloader code
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: On a typical embedded project the firmware effort runs at least twice as long as the hardware effort, and unlike the hardware the scope tends to keep growing, which is the practical argument for getting the board right on the first attempt and absorbing later change in software.
claims.quote_verbatim: the firmware takes at least twice as long

claims.claim_text: Mask-ROM parts make firmware changes destructive to inventory: because the code is fixed at manufacture, any change scraps existing stock, which is why distributors and manufacturers are reluctant to hold mask-programmed devices.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you have to change the firmware, well, you have to scrap all your old stock
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: The practical difference between the older UIO driver and the newer remoteproc driver for a real-time coprocessor is which side loads the firmware: under remoteproc the kernel loads it, whereas UIO left that to a userspace application. The message-passing features layered on remoteproc are optional; memory-mapping the coprocessor and using shared memory as before still works.
claims.quote_verbatim: the kernel loads the firmware rather than the, your, like a user space application loading the firmware on the PRUs
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jason Kridner and Robert Nelson

claims.claim_text: Decompiling a shipped firmware image well enough to locate and correct a defect, and to return a working replacement image, is achievable without access to the hardware or the source, which makes released images a maintenance resource as well as a disclosure risk.
claims.quote_verbatim: He didn't even have one. And he went, right, I've decompiled it. I've fixed... I figured out how it works. I fixed a bug. Here it is. He gave a firmware image back
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Sub-gigahertz radio gateways need region-specific firmware because the licensed band differs by territory: 915 MHz in the United States and Australia against 868 MHz in Europe, and a stock build compiled for one region will not simply work in another.
claims.quote_verbatim: it had to be custom firmware because it's it's an australia specific thing
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Running out of program space converts every later fix into an optimisation exercise: a defect correction had to be paid for by shrinking existing code, and a desirable diagnostic feature showing the firmware revision at power-on could not be added at all.
claims.quote_verbatim: when I went to fix the bug, I was out of program space. So I had to optimize my code to fit the bug fix on there
claims.speaker: Mike Szczys

claims.claim_text: An open-ended contract exposes a firmware consultant to requirement changes that force a processor swap and a full rewrite without a corresponding change to the fee; fixed-bid work is only safe where the finished product has been defined in advance, which is why experienced consultants keep open-scope engagements small.
claims.quote_verbatim: now we have to switch microprocessors and completely rewrite the firmware because it doesn't meet the requirements anymore and they are not willing to rewrite the contract
claims.speaker: Piotr Esden-Tempski

claims.claim_text: Security has to enter at component selection: firmware written for a part with no cryptographic accelerator leaves the implementer performing those operations in software, which is the wrong place for them, and no amount of later software work recovers what the hardware choice gave away.
claims.quote_verbatim: You've, you've written firmware for a part that doesn't have like a crypto core in it and you're like, okay, well, I guess we could do this all in software or in firmware, but that's not the best place to do it
claims.speaker: Josh Datko

claims.claim_text: The security requirements for firmware follow the threat model rather than the product category: a device kept behind guarded physical access can treat physical attack as out of scope, whereas a device carried by users and liable to be lost or stolen cannot, and the two lead to different design choices.
claims.quote_verbatim: if this is like a Bitcoin harder wallet and people, you know, have it in their hands and they can lose it or they can be stolen
claims.speaker: Josh Datko

claims.claim_text: Building a soft processor on an FPGA with a custom peripheral inverts the usual selection problem: rather than hunting for a microcontroller with the right mix of interfaces and then writing intricate firmware that leans on DMA to fake a missing peripheral, the missing peripheral is implemented in fabric and the firmware becomes trivial.
claims.quote_verbatim: instead of writing extremely complex firmware that tries to use DMA controllers and other tricks to speed up bit banging, you end up with something that is a very, very simple firmware because it happens to have the exactly right peripheral for the job
claims.speaker: Claire Wolf

claims.claim_text: Undocumented memory access commands are a common entry point into a radio chip's firmware: given a peek command and a sixteen-bit address space, sweeping the full range from zero to 65535 and disassembling the result recovers the firmware without any physical attack.
claims.quote_verbatim: I found, oh, there's a command that's called peak and poke, which is not documented
claims.speaker: Adrian Studer

claims.claim_text: Firmware committed to unchangeable memory can still be made patchable if it is structured for it, by routing behaviour through indirection points that a later soft patch can redirect; reading how commercial devices do this is a practical source of technique.
claims.quote_verbatim: How can you structure it so you can still have softer patches if you have a bug in that hard-coded firmware
claims.speaker: Adrian Studer

claims.claim_text: Disassembly tooling spans a wide cost range: the free version of the dominant commercial disassembler is limited and a licence covering obscure targets costs a thousand dollars or more, while Radare 2 is free but command-line and steep to learn, and Ghidra, released in 2019, provides a graphical alternative at no cost.
claims.quote_verbatim: it costs you, like, a thousand dollars or more to get a license
claims.speaker: Adrian Studer

claims.claim_text: Reverse engineering firmware proceeds from known anchors outward: identify a byte whose meaning is known from an API call, find where the code compares or writes it, then follow cross-references to that address to infer the purpose of neighbouring code, with each identification constraining the next.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can get cross-references. So you can see what other code is referencing that address I just wrote the frequency to
claims.speaker: Adrian Studer

claims.claim_text: A product that looks simple from outside can spend six months in firmware after the hardware is finished; USB in particular carries far more implementation work than its presence in a specification suggests, and the cost of that choice is only visible after commitment.
claims.quote_verbatim: the hardware has been done for. Oh, hardware's been done for months, six months, you know, and it's been six months or something of, of just like firmware hurdles
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Part numbering can hide an architecture change: GigaDevice's GD32F103 is a register-level match for the STM32F103 and is an ARM device, while the GD32VF103 differs by a single letter and is RISC-V, so firmware and toolchain assumptions carried over from the part number will be wrong.
claims.quote_verbatim: Giga devices decided it was a smart idea to make a completely different architecture part by changing one letter
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Where a vendor publishes firmware updates, those images are the natural starting point for analysis; where none is published, a foothold of code execution can be used to shift the remaining firmware out one bit at a time through an LED or GPIO line, after which the work moves to a disassembler such as Hopper, IDA or Ghidra.
claims.quote_verbatim: some of the other firmware dumps have involved, say, getting a little bit of code execution and then toggling the rest of the firmware out via a LED or a GPIO line
claims.speaker: Trammell Hudson

claims.claim_text: Driving a magnetically deflected vector display requires the firmware to model the deflection coils' inertia: setting the new voltage does not place the beam there immediately, so the code carries tunable delay parameters that keep corners sharp and prevent lines from starting partway along their path.
claims.quote_verbatim: in the firmware for, um, uh, for, for my vector generator, it has some, some, uh, uh, tunable parameters for that sort of thing
claims.speaker: Trammell Hudson

claims.claim_text: Bring-up of a complex board starts at the power supplies before any attempt to run code, and only then moves to the debug interfaces; on a board carrying DDR3, an FPGA, a USB transceiver and a separate power-sequencing microcontroller, that sequencing part is itself the first firmware target.
claims.quote_verbatim: the first thing to check out was the power supplies
claims.speaker: Craig J Bishop
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Craig J Bishop

claims.claim_text: A Zynq-class part boots differently from a plain FPGA: the ARM cores come up first and are responsible for bringing up the fabric, so bring-up runs JTAG to the ARM side, then routes a debug UART out through a companion microcontroller over USB, then ports U-Boot into the boot flash, and only then attempts to boot Linux.
claims.quote_verbatim: you get JTAG access to the ARM side first, and boot up the ARM processors, and make sure those work. And then from there, you can do whatever you want to boot up the FPGA fabric
claims.speaker: Craig J Bishop
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Craig J Bishop

claims.claim_text: An integrated development environment's build console shows the actual compiler invocation and its flags, so an engineer can learn what the toolchain is doing without assembling it by hand; that visibility is what makes the difference between following a vendor's clicks and being able to diagnose a build.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's a console stuff where you can see it actually running the command line, it calls up GCC and then it had includes all of these dash parameters
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Electromagnetic compatibility problems can often be resolved in firmware rather than by respinning the board, which is one reason understanding EMC makes an engineer better at firmware as well as at layout and product design.
claims.quote_verbatim: You can fix EMC problems in firmware
claims.speaker: Jeff Keyzer

claims.claim_text: Simplified beginner environments stop scaling at the point where real debugging is needed, so an engineer moving into firmware seriously has to leave them; deliberate study, paid tutors and a personal project were what one consultant used to make that transition rather than continuing to modify other people's code.
claims.quote_verbatim: I'll just throw an Arduino IDE kind of at this problem or that problem. And it just doesn't work at that point. You know, you don't get debugging
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: The characteristic difficulty of learning firmware is that a failing procedure gives the beginner no way to tell whether the instructions are wrong or their execution of them was; an embedded target is a complete system of parts and memories in which many things can break through no fault of the person following the steps, including mislabelled hardware.
claims.quote_verbatim: as a beginner, if the steps don't work, it could be the way you did it. It could be the steps

claims.claim_text: Firmware is not organised as a discipline in the way computer science is; it is an accumulation of practice built up over three or four decades, largely defined by what silicon vendors have shipped, so there is no mathematically grounded best way to do a given thing, only a peripheral, its registers and its exceptions.
claims.quote_verbatim: Firmware is not a discipline. It's, it's a collection of lore over 30, 40 years

claims.claim_text: Stepping code in a debugger and inspecting the peripheral registers afterwards is what distinguishes a wrong assumption from a wrong implementation; a register believed to be configured may turn out to be untouched because the wrong page was selected, which no amount of print-based debugging reveals cleanly.
claims.quote_verbatim: I thought I set that CRC register. And then I figured out that, no, I, I, I wasn't doing it. I, I, I had the wrong page selected

claims.claim_text: Getting a fabricated chip to the point of being characterised requires a board, assembly, wire bonding, probing and firmware, and that supporting software effort is comparable in size to the chip design itself.
claims.quote_verbatim: then you have to assemble it, wire bond it, put the probe, test it, write firmware for it. Like the software is almost as much work as the chip design
claims.speaker: Adrian Tang

claims.claim_text: A production test can be reduced to loading test firmware, running it once and reading a pass or fail result, provided the measurement circuitry needed to reach that verdict, including temperature and supply monitors, is designed onto the board itself.
claims.quote_verbatim: You load firmware on it, you click run in, and it checks everything, and it gives you a yes or a no
claims.speaker: Adrian Tang

claims.claim_text: Engineers blame the silicon roughly ten times for every one occasion the silicon is actually at fault; the usual resolution is an error in their own firmware. The most common genuine field failure reported against a part is not the part at all but oscillator start-up caused by wrong crystal load capacitors on the customer's board.
claims.quote_verbatim: 10 times I'll say, ah, it's the device. And and I'm ready to go and, you know, write up an errata report. And then I'm like, nope, I made a firmware mistake here
claims.speaker: John Day

claims.claim_text: Where a supporting mechanism such as infrared time synchronisation can be built either elaborately or simply, the elaborate version is the path to failure; keeping it dead simple frees the firmware effort for the part of the product that users actually experience.
claims.quote_verbatim: It turns out the infrared time synchronization stuff, you can make it really complicated, but that is the path towards failure. It turns out the way to do it is actually really dead simple
claims.speaker: Kerry Scharfglass

claims.claim_text: For long-lived installed products, the design divides into parts that are physically hard to change and must last the full service life, and parts deliberately made field-swappable so that software platform changes over many years can be absorbed by replacing a module rather than the installation.
claims.quote_verbatim: the things that are like literally screwed into the side of someone's house will last for as long as they need to last and the stuff that doesn't need to last that long can be swapped
claims.speaker: Kerry Scharfglass

claims.claim_text: The most common failure in embedded projects is beginning to code before the design is settled and documented; the systems that fail catastrophically are usually those where the team did not know clearly what they were building. Systems of around a thousand lines can be coded directly, but at hundreds of thousands or millions of lines that is untenable.
claims.quote_verbatim: The biggest mistake I see people make is to jump into coding too fast
claims.speaker: Jack Ganssle

claims.claim_text: Formal code review, performed before testing rather than after, is the cheapest available route to quality code; the inspection process devised by Michael Fagan in 1976 remains the reference method. A team that installs a good review layer will find fewer defects than expected, because the knowledge that review is coming changes how the code is written.
claims.quote_verbatim: good code reviews are the cheapest way of getting quality code that you can get. Code gets reviewed before it's ever tested
claims.speaker: Jack Ganssle

claims.claim_text: A sole developer with no colleagues to review their code should substitute distance for a second reader: set the code aside for several days or a week before testing it, and commit to craftsmanship in structure and naming conventions on the assumption that the code will still be read in twenty years.
claims.quote_verbatim: put it on the shelf for a few days or a week before you test it
claims.speaker: Jack Ganssle

claims.claim_text: A consultant's firmware deliverable includes its documentation, not merely the binary; treating documentation as part of the product is the first step in bringing firmware work up to the quality-control discipline that hardware deliverables already have.
claims.quote_verbatim: the documentation is as much part of the product as a, you know, as the binary that you release to a client
claims.speaker: Kieran O'Leary

claims.claim_text: Contract work inside an established organisation supplies mutual review between the incoming engineer and the resident hardware or firmware staff, whereas being the sole engineer at a small company removes that check entirely; reviewing one's own work repeatedly reliably fails to catch the defect that matters.
claims.quote_verbatim: you come into a small startup and you're the, the EE or the firmware engineer. And that's, yeah, the buck stops with you
claims.speaker: Alex Klimai

claims.claim_text: In a configurable multi-die part, the interconnect behaviour is determined by firmware held in one-time-programmable memory rather than by the base silicon, so different products share masks while differing in that stored configuration and in the cheaper metallisation layers.
claims.quote_verbatim: which is fundamentally a function of the firmware that's stored in OTP
claims.speaker: Ming Zhang

claims.claim_text: Electronics engineers entering the workforce now routinely do firmware as well as hardware, so they encounter Git regardless; putting hardware design into the same version control system is therefore less a new imposition than an alignment with a tool the same people already have to learn.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you're doing firmware, you're going to want to understand that process anyways, because it's so industry standard for like that firmware software world
claims.speaker: Kyle Dumont
claims.episode_title: Hardware Revision Control with Kyle Dumont

claims.claim_text: The target state for firmware continuous integration is that any commit, however small, is compiled, flashed to a board mounted in a test stand and run through the whole test suite, producing a report; the reason to run every test rather than a selected subset is that the cost of running them is low compared with the cost of an escaped regression.
claims.quote_verbatim: the firmware should get compiled. It should get built. It should get sent to a test board that might be hooked into a test stand
claims.episode_title: Hardware Revision Control with Kyle Dumont

claims.claim_text: Hardware-in-the-loop testing has been run in practice by having a build server push each new firmware build to a machine that then exercises its full range of motion and confirms it does not crash; what makes this harder than software testing is that the assertions depend on real-world measurements and instrumentation.
claims.quote_verbatim: we had a build server and it would push a new version of the code. And we had a, it run through a whole series of unit tests on the printer would go like jog it to all the coordinates and make sure it didn't crash
claims.episode_title: Hardware Revision Control with Kyle Dumont

claims.claim_text: Below roughly ten engineers a company tends to have generalists who do both hardware and firmware; beyond that size dedicated firmware staff appear, while the electronics team increasingly consists of combined electrical and firmware designers doing system-level work.
claims.quote_verbatim: any time a company scales beyond, you know, 10, 10 engineers, you're going to have folks that are just dedicated on, on firmware
claims.speaker: Kyle Dumont
claims.episode_title: Hardware Revision Control with Kyle Dumont

claims.claim_text: A wireless module carrying a vendor Bluetooth stack can accept a bootloader alongside it so that new firmware is delivered over the air or over USB device firmware update, which is what allows a product to be sealed in its case and still be updated.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's like a bootloader that you can put in there, basically
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Keeping the sensor node's firmware to acquisition and light reduction, and running the complex algorithm on a server, makes the firmware much simpler and lets the algorithm be re-run over an existing data set a thousand times instead of requiring a download, flash and wait cycle for each change.
claims.quote_verbatim: get it up to the cloud because computing is nearly free so that all the fermentation algorithms are in the cloud and it makes firmware so much easier
claims.speaker: Eli Hughes

claims.claim_text: On a wireless microcontroller carrying a vendor radio stack, the application firmware is linked at an offset past the memory region the stack occupies and otherwise runs as an ordinary program, so the memory map rather than the code structure is what the developer must get right.
claims.quote_verbatim: It starts at the end of the Bluetooth memory area. And then it just runs like a normal program
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Bluetooth Low Energy is a different protocol from classic Bluetooth and is considerably less flexible; it has no serial port profile, so any product wanting a serial-like link over BLE must construct one over its attribute protocol.
claims.quote_verbatim: Bluetooth LE does not support serial ports over Bluetooth
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Bootloaders must be exceptionally reliable because a failure is unrecoverable in the field, and the compensating advantage is that they generalise well: most of a bootloader, particularly the higher-level update protocol, can be shared across every component in a system with only platform-specific adaptation.
claims.quote_verbatim: bootloaders need to be rock solid, but of course the advantage there is that you can share a lot of that
claims.speaker: Joris Aerts
claims.episode_title: Satellites and EVs with Joris Aerts

claims.claim_text: Simulating a board means instantiating a scripted description of the platform and then loading the same firmware binary that would be flashed to real hardware, so the artefact under test is unchanged and the setup collapses to a few lines of scripting.
claims.quote_verbatim: you just load the binary and you start
claims.speaker: Michael Gielda
claims.episode_title: Simulating Embedded Hardware with Michael Gielda

claims.claim_text: Maintaining forty separate firmware builds that originated as copies of one another means a single defect must be found and corrected in several of them independently; the remedy applied was moving from Subversion to Git with a continuous integration pipeline so the variants share history rather than being duplicated.
claims.quote_verbatim: we have 40 different firmwares that we try to maintain. And a lot of them are just copies of copies of each other. So if you find a bug in one, you might need to fix that one in three, four, five other ones
claims.speaker: Fredrik Kensander
claims.episode_title: High Current Power Supplies with Fredrik Kensander

claims.claim_text: The programming and update story for a connected product has to be decided early, because it determines the firmware architecture, the security model for getting images onto the device and what backend is needed to serve them; deferring it risks omitting something as simple as a device firmware update button that cannot be added later.
claims.quote_verbatim: Is it going to be programmed at the factory? Is it going to be programmed by a technician? Is it going to be programmed over the air
claims.speaker: Jonathan Beri
claims.episode_title: Why IoT Is Difficult with Jonathan Beri

claims.claim_text: The most effective low-power firmware pattern is to wake, complete the work quickly and return to sleep, rather than leaving the processor active while waiting on sensors; gating individual peripherals such as an SPI subsystem within an active burst usually saves so little that a single power-up and power-down per operating mode is the better trade.
claims.quote_verbatim: you want to have the firmware turn on, do its task, and go back to sleep
claims.speaker: Matt Liberty

claims.claim_text: Hardware can be copied but the accumulated firmware and software cannot, so products carrying substantial software development attract clones of the board without direct functional competitors; the same logic applies to functionality held in an FPGA bitstream.
claims.quote_verbatim: they can copy the hardware, right. You know, some company come along and just copy the hardware, but to really, you know, there's a lot of software and firmware that goes into something like this
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: A single incorrect configuration bit in a firmware change can produce a plausible but wrong measurement: flipping the line-frequency setting used for the integration period made readings come out at five sixths of their correct value, an error small enough to survive casual inspection.
claims.quote_verbatim: one day a firmware change had flipped a bit. That was the 50, 60 hertz internal calculation thing
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Some organisations genuinely cannot change processor: without the source for the existing firmware there is no way to produce a functional equivalent, so the decision to migrate has to be taken while the code is still understood.
claims.quote_verbatim: we don't even have the source code to look at in order to, to do a functional equivalent
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: A late architecture change discards prototype work wholesale: a multimeter design that had reached working prototypes on a PIC24F with a suitable LCD driver was scrapped when the manufacturer standardised on ARM, and the firmware was rewritten from scratch after roughly nine months of work.
claims.quote_verbatim: sorry, company's switching to arm. We're switching to arm. We're going to scrap, scrap the pick. We're going to rewrite this from scratch
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: The gap most firmware teams stall in is between building an image automatically and doing anything with it; closing it means having the build system flash a real device and run tests against it, so a failing push is reported as a regression rather than as an unopened artefact.
claims.quote_verbatim: GitHub, flash your device, run the tests, you know, all the, you know, do all the things you want. And if something fails, now you caught a regression
claims.speaker: Akbar Dhanaliwala
claims.episode_title: Firmware Deployment and Troubleshooting with Akbar Dhanaliwala

claims.claim_text: System-level automated tests for firmware go beyond unit tests by exposing a lightweight command shell on a serial port, having the test rig issue single commands such as turning on a heater, and measuring the physical result through an analogue input or an external probe, so the assertion covers the hardware as well as the code.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's a really lightweight shell where if you send it, you can send a different command over you are, you can like turn the heater on
claims.speaker: Akbar Dhanaliwala
claims.episode_title: Firmware Deployment and Troubleshooting with Akbar Dhanaliwala

claims.claim_text: A sealed consumer sensor built around a Bluetooth microcontroller is generally open to anyone with physical access: reaching the JTAG pads allows the firmware to be dumped for analysis and replaced with the owner's own.
claims.quote_verbatim: getting at the JTAG, dumping the firmware and you know, it's a little Bluetooth chip. So at that point you could start to either put your own firmware on there or see what they're doing
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Over-the-air update does not remove the need for an initial programming step at manufacture, and there is no update mechanism for that first load, which makes it the one irreversible point in a product's software lifecycle.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's gotta get programmed once somewhere
claims.speaker: Pete Staples

claims.claim_text: A device that returns a buffer over a bus can be induced to leak its own firmware by corrupting the length field of the transfer, so that the read runs past the buffer and continues through memory into the region where the firmware is mapped.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you corrupt how much to send, it can actually cause it to just continue to read memory. And if the address map is such that the firmware is there, it's also going to read the firmware out of it
claims.speaker: Colin O'Flynn
claims.episode_title: Shouting at chips with Colin O'Flynn

claims.claim_text: Bring-up work sits at the boundary between disciplines: when code will not run, the person doing it must read the schematic with an electrical engineer and confirm the rails come up and the layout is right, because faults such as inverted DRAM line polarity or misrouted battery signals present as firmware failures.
claims.quote_verbatim: the polarity on the DRAM lines is flipped or, you know, the battery signals are routed wrong
claims.speaker: Phillip Johnston
claims.episode_title: Firmware for Hardware Engineers with Phillip Johnston

claims.claim_text: Diagnosing a production line failure means separating four candidate causes: the hardware, the firmware, the test station itself and intermittent behaviour, and narrowing that down requires the hardware skill set as much as the software one.
claims.quote_verbatim: when something fails on the production line, you need to open up the system and look and see what's happening. Try to figure out, is it hardware? Is it the firmware? Is it a problem with the test station? Is it an intermittent issue
claims.speaker: Phillip Johnston
claims.episode_title: Firmware for Hardware Engineers with Phillip Johnston

claims.claim_text: Firmware once required an electrical engineering background, an understanding of computer architecture and habits suited to severely constrained resources; larger memories and frameworks that provide a working foundation have made it practical for software teams to take on embedded projects, leaving board support packages, driver development and power optimisation as the specialist remainder.
claims.quote_verbatim: it used to be to work on firmware. You really did need to be an electrical engineer and like really understand how the hardware worked
claims.speaker: Phillip Johnston
claims.episode_title: Firmware for Hardware Engineers with Phillip Johnston

claims.claim_text: The argument for a digitally controlled power converter is that behaviour lives in firmware: an issue found during validation or after the product is in the field can be addressed by a firmware patch supplied to the customer, whereas the analogue equivalent requires a new silicon spin.
claims.quote_verbatim: you could find a workaround and do a, a, a firmware patch that you give the customer and they can rework the boards
claims.speaker: Carmen Parisi
claims.episode_title: Switching Converter Engineering with Carmen Parisi

claims.claim_text: Substituting a sensor because the original is unobtainable branches the firmware as well as the bill of materials, so a board with many revisions ends up with a matching tree of firmware builds that must be tracked and loaded correctly per unit.
claims.quote_verbatim: Rev A has, you know, this, the BME 280, but Rev B, we can only get the BME 680. And so it's like, so now you have different firmware maybe
claims.speaker: Philip Salmony
claims.episode_title: Mixed Signal Education with Philip Salmony

claims.claim_text: Readout protection on an STM32 has been defeated by fault injection that downgrades the part from RDP level 2 to RDP level 1, which restores debug access limited to RAM; that is sufficient because during a firmware update the private data is copied into RAM to protect it, and can be read there.
claims.quote_verbatim: doing fault injection to re-enable the, the debug interface on the board going from RDP two, which is, you know, read protection to the maximum down to RDP one, which gives you debug access, but only to Ram
claims.speaker: Joe Grand
claims.episode_title: New Life Skills with Joe Grand

claims.claim_text: Hardware wallet firmware has been attacked version by version: one published attack against version 1.7.3 exploited a USB overflow triggered by electromagnetic fault injection, and a separate fault-injection route into the same device was closed in version 1.8, so the security posture of such a product is tied to a specific firmware revision rather than to the model.
claims.quote_verbatim: his attack on, on version 1.7.3, which was a USB kind of overflow issue that he could trigger using electromagnetic fault injection
claims.speaker: Joe Grand
claims.episode_title: New Life Skills with Joe Grand

claims.claim_text: Repeated board spins driven by part availability leave a long tail of firmware conditionals, one per substituted component, and the resulting maintenance cost outlasts and can exceed the immediate cost of the more expensive parts that forced the changes.
claims.quote_verbatim: say you're just switching out the memory that's on board and you have all of these different memories you have to keep now in your firmware and track in your firmware, you get 20, 20 versions that you're pound defining
claims.episode_title: Product Lifecycle Management with Michael Corr

claims.claim_text: A vehicle key fob built on a CC13xx or CC26xx wireless microcontroller had its firmware extracted using side-channel analysis and glitching with an open fault-injection platform, and the image was then reverse engineered with Ghidra.
claims.quote_verbatim: using a chip whisper. So we've had Colin on the show a couple times. This is doing side channel. And glitching. And yeah. Able to. Cool. Dump firmware then. Reverse engineer it using Ghidra
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Where a per-unit secret is stored in the same flash as the application, field updates become impossible, because reprogramming erases the secret along with the code; the firmware must therefore be correct at first programming.
claims.quote_verbatim: I didn't have the option to do field updates because once somebody gets the riddle, it already has like the firmware inside with the secret. And if you like had to re-upload the firmware, then you would override the secret
claims.speaker: Uri Shaked

claims.claim_text: Recording a physical test run once with a logic analyser and replaying it against a simulator turned forty test cases of two to three minutes each into a suite that completed in five seconds, taking the edit-to-result cycle for a firmware change from roughly half a day to seconds.
claims.quote_verbatim: I ended up having a list of 40 different test cases. And each of those tests took like, uh, two minutes to perform
claims.speaker: Uri Shaked

claims.claim_text: Hardware consulting work arrives in discontinuous blocks because each board must be fabricated and assembled before the next task exists, whereas firmware work is continuous; a consultant who adds firmware to their offering smooths both the schedule and the income.
claims.quote_verbatim: there is less of a choppy nature to firmware projects because there's always another thing that needs to be done with firmware
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Replacing a fixed command set with a publish and subscribe model implemented in the device firmware, where the host sends topics and values that the device dispatches individually, removes the need to define a new message every time a control is added; the earlier design processed parameters on the host and became difficult to extend.
claims.quote_verbatim: Now we have actually the device itself processing PubSub in firmware. So we have topics and values that are starting on the host and getting sent down to the device
claims.speaker: Matt Liberty
claims.episode_title: The Joulescope Upgrade with Matt Liberty

claims.claim_text: Industrial controllers are trusted for process control because their firmware is a small, heavily vetted operating system written for one task, unlike a general-purpose computer carrying code bloat, driver problems and forced updates; the practical expectation is that such a controller does not lock up.
claims.quote_verbatim: these are embedded modules that are not only high reliability, but in terms of hardware, but software, the firmware in there as well, their little mini operating system that they run in there
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: A vendor support page for discontinued vector network analysers carried application notes, manuals, calibration kit definitions and firmware images with per-version change logs; when it was removed, web archiving preserved the pages but not the firmware images themselves, so that material is effectively lost to owners of the instruments.
claims.quote_verbatim: it had things like app notes, manuals, but most importantly, firmware images for some of the classic gears with like change logs for the firmware versions
claims.speaker: Jeff Keyzer

claims.claim_text: Firmware that blocks waiting for a peripheral to respond will prevent the whole product from booting whenever that peripheral is unpowered; a device that ran correctly on USB failed to start on battery because the five volt rail the sensor needed was only present when USB was connected.
claims.quote_verbatim: the firmware is waiting for the particulate sensor to come up. But because when it's not plugged into USB, there's no five volts
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: In automotive supply, a subsystem supplier may ship physically identical hardware to competing vehicle makers with entirely different firmware and communication rules, because each maker writes the rules for its own subcontractors and deliberately avoids a shared standard that would permit a second source.
claims.quote_verbatim: It might be the same hardware with completely different firmware
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Battery life is dominated by firmware behaviour rather than by the cell: failing to shut down a peripheral or to enter sleep swamps the design's nominal budget, which is why measuring the current profile against a battery emulator is what connects the power-measurement specialist and the firmware author.
claims.quote_verbatim: firmware has a huge impact on battery life if you missed out to turn off peripherals you forgot to go to sleep
claims.speaker: Werner Johansson
claims.episode_title: Software Defined Power Supplies with Werner Johansson

claims.claim_text: Characterising a cell by discharging it at varying currents and recording the voltage under load reconstructs its internal resistance at each state of charge, and driving that curve from a battery emulator rather than a real pack is what makes firmware power optimisation repeatable; bench instruments of this kind typically step in one percent increments.
claims.quote_verbatim: we needed to do power measurements power optimizations closer to the firmware guys
claims.speaker: Werner Johansson
claims.episode_title: Software Defined Power Supplies with Werner Johansson

claims.claim_text: The closed portion of the Raspberry Pi platform firmware has shrunk over the years to little more than clock and power management, with the graphics side opened and more support moved upstream into the kernel; what remains closed is third-party silicon IP the vendor is not free to publish.
claims.quote_verbatim: If you look at the firmware now, the, the firmware blobs really reduced down to just kind of some clocks and power stuff
claims.speaker: James Adams
claims.episode_title: The RP1 and beyond with the Raspberry Pi Hardware team

claims.claim_text: Two engineers compiling the same firmware source can produce different binaries when their toolchains differ, so building in a shared container or on a build service and distributing that image is what makes the output reproducible across a team.
claims.quote_verbatim: if the tool chain is different or whatever, we might have a different binary
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Layering an embedded system means keeping the firmware to a small, always-correct function such as listening for a signal and switching a relay, and placing policy that changes often at a higher level; writing scheduling logic that will be adjusted daily into C on a microcontroller is what makes such systems unmaintainable.
claims.quote_verbatim: you should basically have some firmware that like just says, listen for signal, flip the relay
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: A configuration-driven firmware generator builds a device image from a declarative description of the attached hardware, which is supportable because the space of valid configurations is known; once a user edits the underlying C or C++ directly, a later refactor of a component will break those local changes and the maintainers cannot support the result.
claims.quote_verbatim: essentially for building firmware for embedded devices that that's customized to support the specific hardware you've attached
claims.speaker: Keith Burzinski
claims.episode_title: Automating the Home with Keith Burzinski

claims.claim_text: A protocol dongle is a microcontroller with a radio running vendor firmware, with the host software driving it over USB; because the device profiles in the protocol are standardised, the host learns a newly paired device's capabilities from the device itself rather than from a driver supplied per product.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's a Silicon Labs. EFR 32 in there, basically. And there's firmware on there
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Vehicle over-the-air update works through a gateway that receives images and distributes them over the internal bus to each of the many microcontrollers, which listen for the update addressed to them; the same modules can also be programmed individually on the bench with a programmer when they are out of the vehicle.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's like basically something that's downloading all the firmware updates and then pushing them over the can
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Safety modules can be serialised to the vehicle in firmware, so a physically identical replacement part does not function until it is programmed to that car; the practical effect is that a mechanical repair becomes a dealer software operation.
claims.quote_verbatim: in the ABS system is bloody firmware integrated with the, and serialized or something. It has to be programmed
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: One low-cost RISC-V microcontroller's debug interface is not a protocol for memory operations but a small scratchpad: the host writes code into it and issues a command, the processor halts the running program and executes that code, and flashing and memory writes are all implemented as short routines sent this way.
claims.quote_verbatim: it gives you access to this, this little scratch pad where you can write code into the scratch pad. And then you send a command and it just executes the code
claims.speaker: CNLohr

claims.claim_text: Rather than maintaining and version-matching a separate firmware image in each satellite chip, a controlling processor can write the code into every peripheral device's RAM at each wake-up, which removes the configuration-tracking problem at the cost of the load time.
claims.quote_verbatim: I just want it to know like, oh, when I wake up, I just have to go write this into all of the chips RAM and then it'll do the right thing
claims.speaker: CNLohr

claims.claim_text: Regulatory pressure has made secure boot and a safe over-the-air upgrade cycle, including a power-on self-test of the image, a requirement rather than an option for general-purpose microcontrollers; all of it rests on a high-assurance initial boot stage, which is where the silicon design effort concentrates.
claims.quote_verbatim: we want to be able to provide secure boot, a safe over the air upgrade cycle, including power on self-test for your image and so on. And it's all kind of built on this foundation of being able to provide a high assurance initial boot
claims.speaker: James Adams
claims.episode_title: The RP2350 with the Raspberry Pi Team

claims.claim_text: Making the boot key unique per device changes the economics of extraction rather than the physics: decapping and fault injection may still recover a key, but the attacker has likely destroyed that unit and gained access to only that one device's firmware, with no leverage over the rest of the fleet.
claims.quote_verbatim: if it's unique per device, well, okay, you can probably, well, you may well have destroyed your device, but if you did get the key, you can probably decode the, the, the firmware
claims.speaker: James Adams
claims.episode_title: The RP2350 with the Raspberry Pi Team

claims.claim_text: A firmware update can change a shipped instrument's behaviour, such as switching a display mode from latched to unlatched to standardise across a product line, but making the behaviour user-selectable requires holding both implementations; on one meter there was insufficient program memory to carry both, so the choice had to be made for the user.
claims.quote_verbatim: we couldn't add that feature because we ran out of ROM space
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Clap on, clap off, lights flicker

claims.claim_text: Connected appliances are typically programmed at the factory with a bootstrap firmware carrying manufacturing test routines, so that an operator with no product knowledge can confirm the motors and indicators work; the device then connects over the network on first use to fetch its current firmware, with user account registration gating which features are enabled.
claims.quote_verbatim: you program with it's you know like a bootstrap firmware that might have like some test software the tests you know the motor and the dishwasher the leds
claims.episode_title: Like a steam engine in your house

claims.claim_text: A root of trust boots an otherwise untrusted system in stages, with a first-stage bootloader in unchangeable ROM verifying the next stage and so on up the chain; the same component subsequently validates firmware updates and signatures, so that a malicious image is rejected rather than merely a corrupted one.
claims.quote_verbatim: you have this one super secure device. That's like checking every stage of the firmware
claims.speaker: Colin O'Flynn
claims.episode_title: Small Scale Electronics Manufacturing with Colin O'Flynn

claims.claim_text: Analysing an unfamiliar connected appliance starts with determining whether it runs Linux or a bare microcontroller, because that decides every subsequent technique; the next question is always whether the firmware can be extracted, after which the system can be unravelled piece by piece.
claims.quote_verbatim: seeing is this, does this run Linux? Is this a microcontroller? And then, uh, digging in and then always asking, you know, Hey, can I get the firmware off of this
claims.speaker: Matt Brown

claims.claim_text: Firmware stored in an eMMC device can be recovered and modified by removing the package from the board, reading and rewriting it externally, and reballing the BGA to reattach it, a physically destructive route used where no software path to the image exists.
claims.quote_verbatim: we're going to be doing some, uh, EMMC chip off and, uh, firmware modification and then doing BGA reballing
claims.speaker: Matt Brown

claims.claim_text: Separating the hardware description from the operational logic, as a device tree does, is what makes changing microcontroller affordable; where pin mappings and controller configuration are embedded directly in the source, unpicking them for a new part is expensive and generates corner-case defects.
claims.quote_verbatim: cost-wise to a company doing a chip change is sometimes a highly draconian process. It is brutally expensive because when hardware description is integrated and embedded into the actual code itself
claims.speaker: Mark Palmeri
claims.episode_title: Medical Electronics Education with Mark Palmeri

claims.claim_text: In a regulated product, moving a classifier from a phone application into the device firmware removes the mobile application, the data transfer path and their security review from the certification scope, so the way to reduce testing burden is to shrink what the system contains rather than to lower the standard applied to it. The cost is pushed back into runtime and battery life on the device.
claims.quote_verbatim: instead of reducing the threshold for any quality or testing rigor we would do, we're looking at changing the scope of the tools we use such that we don't have to add more testing
claims.speaker: Mark Palmeri
claims.episode_title: Medical Electronics Education with Mark Palmeri

claims.claim_text: Language-model assistance on embedded work is effective once the hardware is already up and the device tree and drivers are resolved, where it can build application-level structures such as a menu system or make better use of a real-time operating system's timing primitives; it remains unhelpful for the earlier problem of getting a sensor working at all.
claims.quote_verbatim: once you have it working, now it's like, okay, well, help me build a menu system with this, you know, LED display that I have
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Products shipped without an over-the-air update path and without documentation of their firmware are the ones most exposed to new regulatory requirements, particularly where support obligations extend for years past the end of a product's sale.
claims.quote_verbatim: there are things out there where they just like ship without OTA
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Because a custom chip takes about nine months to return from the fab, the validated RTL is ported to an FPGA with wrappers mapping the design's signals to the FPGA's pins, and the microcontroller firmware that will eventually drive the chip is developed against that FPGA, so the interface between them is debugged before silicon exists.
claims.quote_verbatim: First is the firmware that is going to go on my microcontroller and it's going to talk to the ASIC. Second part, I need the model for my ASIC
claims.speaker: Julia Desmazes
claims.episode_title: Chip Design for Fun (and Waffles) with Julia Desmazes

claims.claim_text: Machine assistance on firmware is currently strong at localised bug fixes and weak at architecting whole systems, so the return depends on recognising early which of the two a task is; the risk is spending longer steering the tool than the work would have taken directly.
claims.quote_verbatim: simple bug fixes and, you know, for firmware or software, it has gotten tremendously good at. You know, architecting full systems, still a big gap
claims.speaker: Matt Liberty
claims.episode_title: AI Tooling with Matt Liberty and Luke Beno

claims.claim_text: Keeping sensor drivers on the Linux host and running a single static firmware load on the sensor node's microcontroller, whose only job is translating wireless commands into I2C or SPI transactions, is what permits sensors to be swapped without reprogramming; putting the drivers on the microcontroller instead makes dynamic swapping impractical because a small part cannot hold every driver.
claims.quote_verbatim: you use the same static firmware load on the microcontroller for all the different sensors, right? Because they are just bus transports
claims.speaker: Jason Kridner

claims.claim_text: For power-constrained remote devices, resolving configuration at build time and reflashing when the requirements change costs less energy than carrying a general runtime-configurable implementation; a virtual machine or container model for updatable code is the alternative where the code genuinely needs to change often.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can update the firmware. Just make the firmware do what you want it to do and configure it ahead of time, right? Configure it at build time, not at runtime
claims.speaker: Jason Kridner

claims.claim_text: Delivering a new capability as a firmware update to hardware the customer already has removes the largest obstacle to evaluation, because the customer is not asked to change their board; a service that works with an ordinary PCB trace antenna at modest efficiency can be tried the day after the offer is made.
claims.quote_verbatim: here's a bit of firmware, do a software update and you can start testing it tomorrow
claims.speaker: Alex Haro
claims.episode_title: Space Age Bluetooth with Alex Haro

claims.claim_text: Not every deployed product needs a network update path: where field technicians already visit the equipment, an update carried on removable media is sufficient, and a device programmed once with information that never changes needs no update mechanism at all.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you have like field technicians with an SD card, they could push a new update by just popping in a new card
claims.speaker: Jonathan Beri
claims.episode_title: Why IoT Is Difficult with Jonathan Beri
